newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. may relax curbs on nuclear sales to China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may relax curbs on nuclear sales to China.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it may allow American companies to sell limited types of nuclear technology to China for peaceful use even before a long-stalled 1985 bilateral agreement is fully implemented.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher made the announcement at the end of day-long talks in which he said China's senior leaders, responding to U.S. concerns, pledged to "formulate and adopt comprehensive nationwide regulations on nuclear export controls".

In recognising this and other progress on curbing the spread of atomic weapons, "the United States is prepared to consider, as consistent with U.S. law, further steps in the area of peaceful nuclear cooperation even in advance of our full implementation of the 1985 agreement", he told a news conference.

U.S. officials said this could mean cooperation in nuclear safety and nuclear reactor development but not "big ticket items" worth billions of dollars like nuclear power reactors themselves, which could only be sold after the 1985 pact is fully in effect.

The announcement was prompted in part because the United States has seen no indication China is violating a May 1996 pledge not to transfer nuclear technology to facilities which are not safeguarded, such as in Pakistan, a senior U.S. official said.

Christopher's first visit to Beijing in more than two years produced no dramatic results. But U.S. officials said it continued forward movement on Sino-American ties, which until recently were spiraling downward due to rows over trade, human rights, Taiwan, nuclear proliferation and arms sales.
More high-level talks were agreed but announcement of summits was deferred, apparently until U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jing Zemin meet on Sunday in Manila.

Differences in many areas remain. Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen warned publicly that tensions over Taiwan could again disrupt Sino-American ties and insisted Washington honour a 1982 commitment to end arms sales to the island.

Christopher said he was not surprised communist China continued to focus on Taiwan, which Bejing considers a renegade regime. Aides said Washington had no intention of halting arms sales to the island.

Christopher said his discussion about China's human rights was "the most high-level coming-to-grips we've ever had" on the issue and he raised the case of prominent dissident Wang Dan, who was imprisoned for 11 years for subversion.
The two sides made no apparent progress on human rights but the issue did not explode into a diplomatic disaster as it did on Christopher's last visit in March 1994.

Washington in 1985 signed with Beijing a pact to allow the transfer of U.S.-made nuclear technology for peaceful uses to China. But the deal was stalled over concerns about China's sale of nuclear items to Iran and Pakistan.
For the pact to take effect, the U.S. president must certify China is not providing nuclear assistance to non-nuclear weapons states with unsafeguarded facilities.
Senior U.S. officials said Clinton is still unable to make this certification and it may be some time before he can.

But China has met some of the eight U.S. requirements for certification and another important step was accomplished Wednesday when Beijing promised to adopt nationwide export controls, one official said. No timetable for action was given.
Beijing has been pressuring the Clinton adminstration to allow American companies to sell China billions of dollars worth of American-made nuclear power reactors.

"The Sino-U.S. agreement on peaceful uses of nuclear technology was signed 11 years ago. We believe it is high time to put this agreement into practice...The China market is very big," said Cui Tiankai, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman.
Chinese leaders also told Christopher they would study joining the 30-member Nuclear Suppliers Group, which decides which nuclear technology requires international safeguards.
The United States and many arms control advocates are keen to draw China into multilateral groupings like that, believing it will encourage behaviour in accord with international norms.
